Exercise A

American Inventions in Numbers

Exercise B

If-Clauses Type 1: Real Possibilities

Choose the correct form. These if-sentences talk about real possibilities: if + present simple, will + verb in the main clause.

If-sentences type 1

1. If you the museum in Menlo Park, you will see Edison's laboratory.

2. If more girls study science, there more female inventors.

3. You will learn a lot about electricity if you this experiment.

4. If a product is really useful, people it.

5. If the battery lasts longer, electric cars more popular.

6. The teacher will be happy if you your project on time.

7. If you are in the laboratory, you touch the machines without permission.

8. If you want to patent an invention, you that it is new.

Exercise C

If-Clauses Type 2: Imaginary Situations

Choose the correct form. These if-sentences talk about unreal or imaginary situations: if + past simple, would + verb in the main clause.

If-sentences type 2

1. If I an inventor, I would build a robot that does homework.

2. If Thomas Edison lived today, he amazed by smartphones.

3. What would you invent if you enough money?

4. If there were no aeroplanes, travelling much longer.

5. If we telephones, communication would be much harder.

6. I would visit Silicon Valley if I to California.

7. If the internet disappeared tomorrow, the world working.

8. Would you buy a flying car if it real?

Exercise D

Writing: The World Without …

Your American partner school is making a wall newspaper called "The World Without …". Write 6–8 sentences for it: choose ONE invention and describe what life would be like without it. Finish with one thing you will invent if you get the chance. Use at least three if-sentences.

Useful phrases
You can use these: If there were no … life would be … people would have to … If I could invent something, … If I get the chance, I will …
Your text
Aim for 6–8 sentences. Use at least 3 if-sentences (type 1 or 2).
